title: Prevalence of diarrhea and its determinants among children under five years of age in rural Kebeles of East Gurage Zone, central Ethiopia: A cross-sectional study
content:
by Melaku Tesfaye, Seid Tiku Mereta, Dessalegn Dadi

Introduction

Diarrheal disease remains a major cause of death among children under five, particularly in resource-limited settings. Despite the availability of effective water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions, the burden of diarrhea remains high in Ethiopia. This study aims to assess the prevalence of diarrhea and its associated factors among under-five children in East Gurage Zone, central Ethiopia.

Methodology

This baseline survey was part of a four-arm cluster randomized trial (cRCT). Using the Hayes and Bennett formula, we set the sample size at 840 participants (210 per arm) with 95% confidence and 80% power. Data were cleaned in Epi Data 3.1 and analyzed in SPSS 25. Reliability testing showed weak internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha of 0.36 for knowledge, 0.46 for practice, and 0.40 for wealth, reflecting few items and distinct domains. Childhood diarrhea associated factors were examined using bivariate and multivariate Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) models, accounting for clustering, with significance set at p < 0.05 and 95% CI.

Results

Diarrhea prevalence was high in the study area (25.7%) (95% CI: 22.8–28.7). Maternal age 24–34 (AOR = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.27–0.53), hand washing at critical times (AOR = 0.20, 95% CI: 0.07–0.58), both soap and water use (AOR = 0.09, 95% CI: 0.03–0.33), using tightly covered (AOR = 0.17, 95% CI: 0.03–0.91) and clean water containers (AOR = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.26–0.84), measles vaccination (AOR = 0.07, 95% CI: 0.04–0.13), fetching water <30 minutes round-trip (AOR = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.12–0.57), and latrine availability (AOR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.19–0.43) were significantly associated with lower odds of under-five diarrhea.

Conclusion

Diarrhea affected one in four children (25.7%; 95% CI: 22.8–28.7), indicating a substantial burden in the study area, particularly in rural communities. Strengthening WASH interventions and fostering coordinated efforts among government, local authorities, and development partners is essential to reduce this burden.
